parakeet: Britannica, for example, describes Mark as the earliest gospel and places it around the period before the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 Common Era. Matthew is generally placed after 70 with dependence on Mark, and Luke is often dated around 63 to 70 CE or later, with other scholarly estimates placing Luke around 80 Common Era. So when apologists say the resurrection was recorded in the Gospels, the response should be no contemporary source records the resurrection event itself. The Gospels are later narrative accounts, not same time documentation. That distinction matters. They were not written the morning after the crucifixion. They were not public records filed by Roman officials. They were not neutral observations from Jerusalem authorities. They were not contemporaneous reports from people standing at the tomb. They're literally theological narratives produced decades later by a movement with a vested interest in presenting a Jesus character as risen, vindicated, and exalted. And we don't have to assume those motives were purely belief in the modern devotional sense. These writings could reflect sincere conviction, community memory, myth making, identity formation, political resistance, theological propaganda, or some combination of all of those. The key point is not that the authors were lying or just believers. The key point is that these texts emerge from within a developing movement after the fact. So the stronger critique is the gospels do not give us contemporary documentation of the resurrection. They give us later Christian narrative claims about the resurrection. The event itself is not contemporaneously documented in any surviving source, insider or outsider.
